title: How do you get good visuals from one promt?
author: KingCakeTheFruity
selftext:
Here and there I see people getting juicy procedural visuals or UI effects from some simple efforts. I do a ton of prototyping, and it works wonders in terms of mechanics - any complex logic, compute shaders and so on are produced effortlessly with Codex. But as soon as I say  "make it look good", the results are usually SO bad that it sometimes includes this in the report, like "this is a rough prototype, so I decided not to create any animations, although I know that's what you asked for". 

So what is the secret visual pipeline you use to get really pretty results without explaining each tween individually? 

I'm working with Godot + Codex if this matters

comments.author: lollyadorable4
comments.body: In my experience "make it look good" is too vague for it to have anything to anchor to. Naming a specific style or reference (like "cel-shaded, Hollow Knight-ish palette") tends to help way more than just saying "good". Also breaking it into passes helps, get the shape/animation logic first, then a separate pass just for materials/lighting/juice instead of asking for both at once.

replies.author: KingCakeTheFruity
replies.body: That's totally true, but even the requests like "search the internet on how a good [for example] slot-machine effects work and use it as reference" don't help, it gets the references and produce pure nonsense, like shifting the icons completely out of their cells for this slot machine example. I understand there's no way to help with no context here, but I wanted to hear some "general advice on getting better visuals", so thanks for your answer!

replies.author: lollyadorable4
replies.body: Ur welcome! I think the core issue is you're asking a coding agent to nail visual quality purely from text description, without any visual feedback loop. Some tools let the agent take a screenshot of the actual render and iterate off that directly, instead of you having to describe every tween/effect in words. That closes the gap a lot more than just better prompting does, since the agent can literally see what looks off and adjust.
